label: Blue Note
rationale: Mosaic (1961) is one of the defining hard-bop records of the Blue Note catalogue: the first studio date by the celebrated Shorter-Hubbard-Fuller front line with the Cedar Walton-Jymie Merritt-Art Blakey rhythm section. Recorded in a single October 2, 1961 session at Van Gelder Studio, it pairs five original compositions (by Walton, Hubbard, Shorter and Fuller) with a sextet whose personnel network sits at the center of the 1960s hard-bop tradition. Consensus is strong and independent: AllMusic rates it four-and-a-half stars (review by Thom Jurek), the Penguin Guide to Jazz Recordings four stars, and the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide four stars (ratings as transcribed in Wikipedia's review-score table, S2). It is one of the most frequently cited Jazz Messengers albums and a standard-bearer of the hard-bop sextet sound. style_primary 'hard-bop' per AllMusic's sole style tag (S1) and Wikipedia's genre (S2).

personnel_record.notes: Single session, October 2, 1961, Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, NJ (S1, S2, S3). Blue Note BLP 4090 (mono) / BST 84090 (stereo) (S3). Wikipedia infobox dates the release January 1962 while AllMusic lists release year 1961 (S1, S2); the 1961 session/catalog year is used. Producer Alfred Lion and engineer Rudy Van Gelder (recording and mastering) per Wikipedia technical personnel (S2), corroborated by AllMusic credits (S1). AllMusic recording location shows a 'New York, NY' city line alongside 'The Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, NJ' (S1) - the studio is in Englewood Cliffs, NJ, not New York City (a known AllMusic city-label quirk); site resolved to van-gelder-studio-englewood-cliffs on the post-July-1959 session date. No alternate takes; the session yielded exactly the five issued tracks (S2). Durations per Wikipedia (S2); AllMusic lists total 39:39 (S1) vs Wikipedia 40:16 (S2) - minor transfer/timing variance.

ballot.album: Art Blakey & The Jazz Messengers — Mosaic (1961)
ballot.case_for: Mosaic is the studio debut of the Shorter–Hubbard–Fuller–Walton–Merritt–Blakey sextet — the most-cited Jazz Messengers configuration and the moment the band expanded from quintet to a thicker, more orchestral three-horn front line. Three independent rating traditions converge at the top tier (AllMusic 4.5 stars, Penguin Guide 4 stars, Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 4 stars). Every track is a band-member original, making the album a composer's workshop for the emerging post-bop generation: Walton's title track, Shorter's 'Children of the Night,' Hubbard's 'Down Under' and 'Crisis,' Fuller's 'Arabia.' The session gravity is immense — Hubbard, Shorter, and Fuller each went on to define the 1960s Blue Note catalogue.
ballot.case_against: Mosaic is a peak-quality session but not the band's most iconic record: Moanin' (1958) and Free for All (1964) both make stronger claims as the Messengers' defining statement. The album perfects an established hard-bop formula rather than pushing the lineage forward — its organizing principle is squarely within the lane Blakey had already paved. The dossier's sourcing is also partly mediated: the Penguin Guide and Rolling Stone ratings reach the dossier through Wikipedia's review-score table rather than primary sources, and the claim of being 'one of the most frequently cited Jazz Messengers albums' is asserted without a single NPR/JazzTimes/DownBeat canon list or musician-citation trail.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes consensus_core at strong priority — the Shorter–Hubbard–Fuller front line's studio debut carries overwhelming session gravity and three-source consensus, but the dossier's 'defining record of the Blue Note catalogue' rhetoric should be tempered to 'defining lineup debut' before John records this.
